tool.name: Regular expressions
tool.tagline: A compact pattern language for searching, validating and rewriting text
tool.description: Regular expressions describe sets of strings with a few dozen symbols, and nearly every language, editor and command-line tool supports them. Learn them once to search code, extract fields from logs, validate input and do bulk search-and-replace, and learn their limits so they never become a bug or a security hole.

glossary.def: In regular expressions, the text you write to describe what to look for, such as \d+ for 'one or more digits'. The program then finds every piece of text that fits it.
In regular expressions, what parentheses do: they remember the exact text their part of the pattern matched, so a program can read it out (group 1, group 2...) or reuse it.
The programming language that runs inside web browsers (and on servers with Node.js). It has regular expressions built in, written between slashes like /\d+/.
A character with a special meaning in a regular expression, such as . * + ? ( ) [ ] { } | ^ $ or \. Put a backslash in front to match it as an ordinary character.
The code inside a programming language or tool that takes a regular expression and actually searches text with it.
A set of characters in square brackets, like [aeiou] or [0-9], that matches exactly one character from the set. [^...] matches any character not in it.
A symbol after part of a regex saying how many times it may repeat: * (zero or more), + (one or more), ? (zero or one) or {m,n}.
A quantifier followed by ?, such as *? or +?, which matches as few characters as possible instead of as many as possible.
The regex \b: the position between a word character (letter, digit, underscore) and anything else, such as a space or the end of the text.
Choosing between alternatives with | in a regular expression: cat|dog matches cat or dog.
A group written (?:...) that bundles part of a regex, for example so a quantifier applies to all of it, without remembering the text it matched.
A capturing group given a name, (?<name>...) or (?P<name>...) in Python, so code can read its text by name instead of by number.
What a successful regex search returns in Python or JavaScript: the matched text, where it was found, and the text of each group.
\1 (or \k<name>) inside a regex: it matches exactly the same text that an earlier group captured, such as a repeated word.
A regex check of what comes right after (lookahead) or before (lookbehind) the current position, without including that text in the match.
A part of a regex that checks a condition at a position, such as ^, \b or a lookaround, without matching any characters.
A group written (?>...): once it has matched, the regex engine won't go back and try matching it differently.
A quantifier followed by +, such as *+ or ++: it takes as much as it can and never gives any of it back.
How most regex engines work: try one way of matching, and when it fails, go back to the last choice and try the next option.
When a regex can match the same text in a huge number of ways and the match then fails, so the engine tries them all and can take years on a short input.
Regular expression denial of service: an attack that sends text which makes a vulnerable regex run for a very long time, freezing the program.
One dialect of regular expressions, such as POSIX, PCRE, JavaScript, Python or RE2. They share the basics but differ in syntax and features.
Perl Compatible Regular Expressions: the widely used regex library and dialect, with the richest feature set, used by PHP, grep -P, nginx and others.
Google's regex engine, and the family of engines like it (Go, Rust), that guarantees matching time grows only in proportion to the text, by leaving out backreferences and lookarounds.
One character as a reader sees it, such as é or a family emoji, which may be stored as several Unicode code points.
A regex class like \p{L} (any letter) or \p{Script=Greek} that selects characters by their Unicode category or writing system.
A switch that changes how a whole regular expression behaves, such as i to ignore upper and lower case, or m to make ^ and $ work on each line.
A regex flag (m) under which ^ and $ match at the start and end of every line, not just of the whole text.

In computer science, a set of strings that can be recognised by reading the text once while remembering only a fixed, limited amount of information. Classic regular expressions describe exactly these.
A simple machine made of a fixed number of states, moving from state to state as it reads each character. Every classic regular expression can be turned into one.
Non-deterministic finite automaton: a state machine that may be in several states at once. Simulating all of them together lets an engine match a regex in time proportional to the text's length.
Deterministic finite automaton: a state machine that is always in exactly one state, so matching is one table lookup per character, but it can need very many states.
A quantifier's default behaviour: take as many characters as possible, then give some back only if the rest of the pattern needs them.

concepts.name: Literals, metacharacters and escaping
concepts.summary: A regex is a search pattern for text: most characters match themselves, a dozen special characters mean something else, and a backslash makes them ordinary.
concepts.why: Every other regex feature builds on knowing which characters stand for themselves and which are special.
concepts.body:
A **regular expression** (**regex** for short) is a small pattern that describes the text you're looking for. You've used a plain search box: type `cat` and it finds `cat`. A regex search works the same way, but the pattern can also say things like "any digit here" or "one or more letters". Most programming languages and text editors support regexes.

Programmers call a piece of text a **string**. A part of the string that fits the pattern is a **match**. Most characters in a pattern simply match themselves: the pattern `cat` finds `cat` inside `concatenate`.

A few characters are **metacharacters**, with special meanings you'll learn over the next lessons:

```
.  ^  $  *  +  ?  (  )  [  ]  {  }  |  \
```

To match one of them as an ordinary character, **escape** it: put a backslash `\` in front. `3\.14` matches `3.14` but not `3x14`, because an unescaped `.` means "any character". `\(` matches a real parenthesis. Inside square brackets `[...]` (next lesson) most of them lose their special meaning, so `[.]` also matches a real dot.

The examples use **Python**, a popular **programming language** (a language for writing instructions a computer carries out). You only need to read three things: `re.search(pattern, text)` finds the first match, `re.findall(pattern, text)` lists every match, and `print(...)` shows a result, which the examples repeat after `#`.

Two ideas to keep in mind from the start:

- Matching is usually a **search**: the pattern may match anywhere in the text unless you pin it to the start or end (a later lesson). Python has both: `re.search` looks anywhere, while `re.fullmatch` requires the whole text to match.
- In program code, text is written between quotes, and backslashes inside quotes already have their own meaning there. To keep a pattern's backslashes exactly as typed, Python uses a **raw string**, written with an `r` before the opening quote: `r"\d+"`. JavaScript writes patterns between slashes instead: `/\d+/`.

When the text you want to find comes from someone else, such as a word a person typed into a form, don't add backslashes by hand: Python's `re.escape()` (or your language's equivalent) adds every one that's needed.
concepts.code:
import re

print(re.search(r"cat", "concatenate"))      # <re.Match object; span=(3, 6), match='cat'>  found at position 3
print(re.findall(r"3.14", "3.14 3x14"))      # ['3.14', '3x14']  . matches any character
print(re.findall(r"3\.14", "3.14 3x14"))     # ['3.14']
print(re.fullmatch(r"cat", "concatenate"))   # None: the whole text must match

user_input = "1+1=2?"
pattern = re.escape(user_input)
print(pattern)                               # 1\+1=2\?
print(bool(re.search(pattern, "is 1+1=2?"))) # True
takeaways: Most characters match themselves; . ^ $ * + ? ( ) [ ] { } | \ are special
Put \ in front of a special character (or put it inside [ ]) to match it as an ordinary character
In Python, write patterns as raw strings, r"...", and use re.escape for text someone else typed
pitfalls: Searching for a version like 1.2.3 without escaping the dots, so the pattern also matches 1x2y3.

quiz.q: Which pattern matches only the exact text a+b?
quiz.explain: + is special (it means 'one or more', as the next lessons show), so it must be escaped to match a real plus sign.

concepts.name: Character classes
concepts.summary: Match one character from a set with [abc], ranges like [a-z], 'anything but' with [^...], the shortcuts \d \w \s, and the dot.
concepts.why: Character classes are how a pattern says 'a digit here, a letter there', the core of almost every useful regex.
concepts.body:
A **character class**, written in square brackets, matches exactly **one** character from a set:

- `[aeiou]` one vowel; `[a-z]` any character in a range (here, a lowercase letter); `[A-Za-z0-9_]` several ranges together.
- `[^0-9]` a **negated** class: any character except a digit, including the invisible **line break** character (newline) that ends each line.
- Inside a character class, `^` is special only at the start, `-` only between two characters (put it first or last to mean a real hyphen), and `]` must be escaped or come first.

Shortcuts save typing:

- `\d` a digit, `\w` a "word character" (letter, digit or underscore), `\s` **whitespace**: a space, tab, line break or other invisible spacing.
- Capital versions mean the opposite: `\D`, `\W`, `\S`.
- `.` matches any character **except a line break** (unless the dotall flag, a later lesson, is on).

Which characters count as digits and letters? Computers store each character as a number. The old **ASCII** standard numbers only English letters, digits and common symbols; **Unicode** covers every writing system in the world.

In Python 3 (and in JavaScript with the `u` or `v` flag), `\d` and `\w` follow Unicode: Python's `\d` also matches digits from other writing systems, such as the Arabic-Indic `٣`. Use `[0-9]` (or Python's `re.ASCII` flag) when you mean only 0 to 9, for example when checking that someone typed a number.

Classic Unix text tools such as grep and sed, which follow the older **POSIX** standard, use bracket names like `[[:digit:]]` and `[[:space:]]` instead of the backslash shortcuts.
concepts.code:
import re

text = "Room 101, floor 3; code A-7_x"
print(re.findall(r"\d", text))            # ['1', '0', '1', '3', '7']
print(re.findall(r"[A-Z]", text))         # ['R', 'A']
print(re.findall(r"[^a-z0-9 ]", text))    # ['R', ',', ';', 'A', '-', '_']
print(re.findall(r"[-_]", text))          # ['-', '_']   hyphen first = a real hyphen
print(re.findall(r"\s", "a b\tc"))        # [' ', '\t']

print(re.findall(r"\d", "٣ and 3"))               # ['٣', '3']  Unicode digit
print(re.findall(r"\d", "٣ and 3", re.ASCII))     # ['3']
print(re.findall(r"[0-9]", "٣ and 3"))            # ['3']
takeaways: [...] matches exactly one character from the set; [^...] means any character but these
\d \w \s are shortcuts; \D \W \S mean the opposite
. matches anything except a line break by default
pitfalls: Writing [a-Z] or [A-z]: the second also includes [ \ ] ^ _ and backtick, which sit between Z and a.

quiz.q: How many characters does [abc]+ need to match at minimum, and how many does [abc] match?
quiz.explain: A class always matches a single character; + then requires at least one repetition.

concepts.name: Quantifiers: * + ? and {m,n}
concepts.summary: Repeat the previous item with * (zero or more), + (one or more), ? (optional) and {m,n} (bounded counts).
concepts.why: Quantifiers let one pattern match inputs of different lengths, such as numbers, words and optional parts.
concepts.body:
A **quantifier** follows an item (a character, a character class, or a group in parentheses) and says how many times it may repeat:

- `*` zero or more: `ab*c` matches `ac`, `abc`, `abbbc`.
- `+` one or more: `\d+` matches a whole run of digits.
- `?` zero or one, i.e. optional: `colou?r` matches `color` and `colour`.
- `{3}` exactly three, `{2,4}` two to four, `{2,}` two or more.

A quantifier applies only to the **single item** right before it. `ab+` means `a` followed by one or more `b`s; to repeat a sequence, group it: `(ab)+` matches `ababab`.

By default quantifiers are **greedy**: they take as much text as possible while still letting the whole pattern match. That is usually what you want for runs of digits or letters, and it causes the classic `.*` surprises covered in the lesson on greedy and lazy quantifiers.

Be careful with patterns that can match **nothing at all** (an empty string, zero characters long), like `\d*`. They "succeed" at positions where nothing interesting is present, so `re.findall(r"\d*", "a1")` returns empty matches as well as `'1'`. Prefer `+` when you need at least one character.
concepts.code:
import re

print(re.findall(r"ab*c", "ac abc abbbc"))      # ['ac', 'abc', 'abbbc']
print(re.findall(r"\d+", "order 66 of 1977"))  # ['66', '1977']
print(re.findall(r"colou?r", "color colour"))  # ['color', 'colour']
print(re.findall(r"\b\d{4}\b", "in 1977, 42, 12345"))  # ['1977']  (\b marks a word's edge: later lesson)
print(re.findall(r"(?:ab)+", "abababx ab"))     # ['ababab', 'ab']  (?:ab) groups ab: later lesson

print(re.findall(r"\d*", "a1"))                 # ['', '1', '']  empty matches!
print(re.findall(r"\d+", "a1"))                 # ['1']
takeaways: * zero or more, + one or more, ? optional, {m,n} bounded
A quantifier applies to the one item before it; group to repeat a sequence
Quantifiers are greedy by default
pitfalls: Using * where + was meant, so the pattern also matches the empty string.

quiz.explain: {2,3} applies to the a alone, so the string is h followed by two or three a's.

concepts.name: Anchors and word boundaries
concepts.summary: Pin matches to positions with ^ and $ (start and end), \b word boundaries and \A \z for the absolute string ends.
concepts.why: Without anchors, a validation pattern accepts any string that merely contains a valid part.
concepts.body:
**Anchors** match a position between characters, not a character, so they use up no text:

- `^` start of the string (or of each line, with the multiline flag from a later lesson).
- `$` end of the string (or of each line, with the multiline flag). In Python, and in **PCRE** (another widely used kind of regex), `$` also matches just before a final line break; in JavaScript it doesn't.
- `\b` a **word boundary**: between a word character (`\w`) and a non-word character or the string edge. `\bcat\b` finds `cat` but not `concatenate`. `\B` is the opposite.
- `\A` and `\z` (Python: `\A` and `\Z`) always mean the very start and very end of the string, regardless of flags.

Anchors are essential for **validation**: checking that a whole piece of text has the right form. `\d{5}` finds five digits inside `"abc123456"`, so it would accept that string as a ZIP code; `^\d{5}$` requires the whole string to be five digits. In Python `re.fullmatch(r"\d{5}", s)` does the same without anchors and avoids the final-line-break quirk of `$`.

Word boundaries depend on what counts as `\w`, so `\b` treats `-` and `'` as boundaries: `\bcan\b` matches inside `can't`.
concepts.code:
import re

print(re.findall(r"cat", "cat concatenate"))       # ['cat', 'cat']
print(re.findall(r"\bcat\b", "cat concatenate"))   # ['cat']

zip_re = re.compile(r"^\d{5}$")                   # prepare the pattern once, reuse it
print(bool(re.search(r"\d{5}", "abc123456")))      # True  (contains five digits)
print(bool(zip_re.search("abc123456")))           # False
print(bool(zip_re.search("12345")))               # True
print(bool(zip_re.search("12345\n")))             # True!  $ allows a final newline
print(bool(re.fullmatch(r"\d{5}", "12345\n")))    # False

lines = "error: a\nok\nerror: b"
print(re.findall(r"^error: (\w)", lines, re.MULTILINE))   # ['a', 'b']  (the ( ) returns just that letter)
takeaways: ^ and $ anchor to the start and end; \b to word edges
Validation patterns must be anchored (or use fullmatch)
In Python and PCRE, $ also matches before a final newline
pitfalls: Checking typed-in text with a pattern that has no anchors, which accepts anything that merely contains a valid part.

options: Search finds three digits anywhere because the pattern isn't anchored
quiz.explain: Without ^ and $ the pattern can match any three consecutive digits inside the string.

concepts.name: Alternation and grouping
concepts.summary: Match one of several alternatives with |, and use parentheses to group parts so quantifiers and alternation apply to them.
concepts.why: Grouping controls what belongs together; most confusing regex bugs come from | applying to more than intended.
concepts.body:
The `|` character means **or**: `cat|dog` matches either word. It binds more loosely than anything else in a pattern (it has the **lowest priority**), so it splits the entire pattern, or the group around it, into alternatives. `^cat|dog$` is "`cat` at the start, or `dog` at the end", not "the whole string is cat or dog".

Parentheses **group** things:

- to limit alternation: `^(cat|dog)$`, `gr(a|e)y`;
- to apply a quantifier to a sequence: `(ha)+`, `(\d{1,3}\.){3}\d{1,3}`;
- to **capture**: remember the text that part matched, so a program can read it out (next section).

If you only need grouping, not capturing, write a **non-capturing group** `(?:...)`. Captured parts are numbered 1, 2, 3..., and leaving out the ones you don't need keeps that numbering simple. In Python, `findall` returns the groups instead of the whole match when the pattern contains capturing groups, which is another reason to prefer `(?:...)` for pure grouping.

Most **regex engines** (the code inside a language or tool that runs your pattern) try alternatives **left to right** and take the first that leads to an overall match, not the longest. So `in|int` against `"integer"` matches `in`. Put longer alternatives first, or add boundaries: `\b(?:int|in)\b`. POSIX tools like grep return the leftmost-longest match instead.
concepts.code:
import re

print(re.findall(r"cat|dog", "hotdog catalog"))           # ['dog', 'cat']
print(bool(re.search(r"^cat|dog$", "catalog")))           # True: ^cat matched
print(bool(re.search(r"^(?:cat|dog)$", "catalog")))       # False
print(re.findall(r"gr(?:a|e)y", "gray grey groy"))        # ['gray', 'grey']
print(re.findall(r"(?:ha)+", "hahaha!"))                  # ['hahaha']

print(re.search(r"in|int", "integer").group())            # in   (first alternative wins)
print(re.search(r"int|in", "integer").group())            # int

print(re.findall(r"(ha)+", "hahaha"))     # ['ha']  findall returns the captured part!
takeaways: | has the lowest priority: group alternatives with ( )
Use (?:...) when you need grouping but not capturing
Most engines take the first alternative that works, not the longest
pitfalls: Writing ^yes|no$ for 'yes or no only' instead of ^(?:yes|no)$.

options: jpg at the start or png at the end
Any string containing jpg or png
quiz.explain: The group confines the alternation, and both anchors apply to whichever alternative matched.

concepts.name: Capture groups and named groups
concepts.summary: Extract parts of a match with numbered (...) and named (?P<name>...) or (?<name>...) groups, and read them from the match object.
concepts.why: Pulling labelled pieces out of program logs, dates and web links is the most common real use of regex.
concepts.body:
Each pair of capturing parentheses remembers the text it matched. Afterwards your code reads that text from the **match object**, the result a successful search returns. Groups are numbered by their **opening parenthesis**, left to right, starting at 1; group 0 is the whole match.

**Named groups** make patterns self-documenting and robust to edits:

- Python: `(?P<year>\d{4})`, and since 3.12 also `(?<year>\d{4})`; read with `m["year"]` or `m.groupdict()`.
- JavaScript, PCRE, .NET, Java: `(?<year>\d{4})`; in JS read `m.groups.year`.

Details worth knowing:

- A group inside a quantifier keeps only its **last** iteration: `(\d)+` on `"123"` captures `3`.
- An optional group that didn't participate returns `None` in Python and `undefined` in JavaScript.
- `findall` returns each match's groups bundled together, like `('x', '1')`, when there are several; `finditer` gives full match objects one by one, which is usually clearer.
- Prefer non-capturing `(?:...)` for groups you don't read, so numbering stays stable.

When you use the same pattern many times, prepare it once with `re.compile` and loop over `finditer`. When the data is in a real data format, such as JSON or the CSV spreadsheet format, use a reader made for that format instead (see the lesson on when not to use regex); regex extraction is best for loosely structured text like log lines.
concepts.code:
import re

line = "2026-10-17 12:04:55 ERROR [db] connection lost"
pat = re.compile(r"(?P<date>\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}) \S+ (?P<level>[A-Z]+) \[(?P<src>\w+)\]")
m = pat.search(line)
print(m.group(0))          # 2026-10-17 12:04:55 ERROR [db]
print(m["level"], m[3])    # ERROR db
print(m.groupdict())       # {'date': '2026-10-17', 'level': 'ERROR', 'src': 'db'}

print(re.search(r"(\d)+", "123").group(1))       # 3  (last iteration)
print(re.search(r"(a)?b", "b").group(1))         # None

for m in re.finditer(r"(\w+)=(\d+)", "x=1 y=22"):
    print(m.group(1), int(m.group(2)))           # x 1 / y 22
takeaways: Groups are numbered by their opening parenthesis; group 0 is the whole match
Named groups: (?P<name>...) in Python, (?<name>...) almost everywhere
A repeated group keeps only its last repetition
pitfalls: Expecting (\d)+ to capture every digit; capture the whole run with (\d+) instead.

quiz.explain: Numbering follows opening parentheses: 1 is (ab), 2 is (a), 3 is (b).

concepts.name: Greedy versus lazy quantifiers
concepts.summary: Understand why .* overshoots, how lazy quantifiers *? +? ?? take as little as possible, and why a negated class is often better.
concepts.why: The single most common regex bug is a greedy .* swallowing far more text than intended.
concepts.body: Greedy quantifiers grab as much as they can, then **give back** characters one at a time until the rest of the pattern matches. With `<.+>` on `bold`, `.+` first runs to the end of the string, then backs off until it finds the last `>`, so the match is the whole `bold`. Adding `?` makes a **lazy quantifier** (also called reluctant): `*?`, `+?`, `??`, `{m,n}?`. A lazy quantifier takes as little as possible and expands only when the rest of the pattern fails. `<.+?>` matches `` and then ``. Often an even better fix is a **negated character class** that can't cross the closing character: `<[^>]+>`. It says exactly what you mean ("everything up to the next `>`"), it never backtracks across delimiters, and it behaves the same in engines without lazy quantifiers (POSIX grep and sed). Laziness changes which match is found, not where the search starts: matches are still found leftmost first. `a.*?b` on `xaab` matches `aab`, starting at the first `a`. Remember that `.` doesn't match newlines by default, so `.*` stops at the end of a line; that's a frequent reason a multi-line extraction "doesn't work".
concepts.code: import re html = "bold and italic" print(re.findall(r"<.+>", html)) # ['bold and italic'] print(re.findall(r"<.+?>", html)) # ['', '', '', ''] print(re.findall(r"<[^>]+>", html)) # ['', '', '', ''] s = 'name="Ana" city="Rome"' print(re.findall(r'"(.*)"', s)) # ['Ana" city="Rome'] print(re.findall(r'"(.*?)"', s)) # ['Ana', 'Rome'] print(re.findall(r'"([^"]*)"', s)) # ['Ana', 'Rome'] print(re.search(r"a.*?b", "xaab").group()) # aab (leftmost start wins)
takeaways: Greedy quantifiers take the most, then give back; lazy quantifiers take the least
Add ? to make a quantifier lazy: *? +? ?? {m,n}?
A negated class like [^"]* is often clearer and faster than .*?
pitfalls: Using ".*" to match a quoted string on a line that contains several quoted strings.

quiz.explain: The greedy .* runs to the last closing parenthesis, capturing everything between the first ( and the last ).

quiz.q: Which pattern extracts the contents of each pair of square brackets most robustly?
quiz.explain: The negated class can't cross a closing bracket, so each pair is matched separately.

concepts.name: Flags: case, multiline, dotall, verbose
concepts.summary: Change matching behaviour with flags: ignore case, ^/$ per line, dot matches newline, verbose patterns with comments, and JavaScript's g, y, u, v and d.
concepts.why: Flags fix the most common 'why doesn't it match across lines?' problems and make long patterns readable.
concepts.body:
**Regex flags** (also called modifiers) change how a whole pattern behaves. The common ones exist in most flavours under similar letters:

- `i` ignore case. Python: `re.IGNORECASE`.
- `m` **multiline mode**: `^` and `$` match at every line start and end, not just the string ends. Python: `re.MULTILINE`.
- `s` **dotall**: `.` also matches newline. Python: `re.DOTALL`.
- `x` **verbose**: whitespace in the pattern is ignored and `#` starts a comment, so complex patterns can be laid out over several lines. Python: `re.VERBOSE`; not available in JavaScript.

Flags can also be set inside the pattern: `(?i)abc`, or scoped to a group as `(?i:abc)`. Python requires global inline flags at the very start of the pattern.

JavaScript adds flags of its own:

- `g` global: needed for `matchAll` and for `replace` to change every match. It makes the regex remember where its last match ended (in its `lastIndex` property), which surprises people who reuse a `/g` regex with `test()`.
- `y` sticky: match only at `lastIndex`.
- `u` Unicode mode and `v` (ES2024) its stricter successor, which allows set operations inside character classes.
- `d` records where each group starts and ends.

Combine flags with `|` in Python (`re.I | re.M`) or by listing letters in JavaScript (`/x/gimu`).
concepts.code:
import re

text = "Title\nfirst line\nSecond line"
print(re.findall(r"^\w+", text))                    # ['Title']
print(re.findall(r"^\w+", text, re.M))              # ['Title', 'first', 'Second']
print(re.findall(r"line$", text, re.M | re.I))      # ['line', 'line']
print(re.search(r"Title.*line", text))              # None: . stops at \n
print(re.search(r"Title.*line", text, re.S).group().count("\n"))   # 2

phone = re.compile(r'''
    \(?(\d{3})\)?   # area code, optional parentheses
    [\s.-]?         # separator
    (\d{3})[\s.-]?(\d{4})
''', re.VERBOSE)
print(phone.search("call (555) 123-4567").groups())  # ('555', '123', '4567')
takeaways: i ignores case, m makes ^ $ per line, s lets . match newlines
Verbose mode (x) allows whitespace and comments inside the pattern
In JavaScript, g makes a regex remember its position in lastIndex
pitfalls: Reusing a /g regex with test() in JavaScript and getting alternating true/false because lastIndex moved.

quiz.q: You need ^ to match at the start of every line of a log. Which flag?
quiz.explain: Multiline mode makes ^ and $ match at line boundaries inside the string.

concepts.name: Search and replace with groups
concepts.summary: Rewrite text with re.sub and String.replace, refer to groups as \1, \g<name>, $1 or $<name>, and use a function for computed replacements.
concepts.why: Bulk edits, data cleaning and format conversion are all search-and-replace with groups.
concepts.body:
Every language's regex tools can also replace matches, and the replacement text can refer to captured groups. How you write that differs:

- Python `re.sub`: `\1`, `\g<1>` or `\g<name>`. Use `\g<1>0` when a digit follows, since `\10` would mean group 10.
- JavaScript `replace`/`replaceAll`: `$1`, `$<name>`, `$&` for the whole match, `$$` for a real dollar sign.
- sed: `\1` and `&`; editors such as VS Code use `$1`.

Instead of replacement text you can pass a **function** (a small named piece of code; in the example, a one-line `lambda`) that receives the match and returns the replacement. Use it when the new text has to be computed: converting units, changing case, looking values up in a table.

Other useful knobs:

- Python `re.sub(p, r, s, count=1)` limits the number of replacements; `re.subn` also returns how many were made.
- In JavaScript, `replace` with a string pattern or a regex without `g` replaces only the first match; use the `g` flag or `replaceAll`.
- Escape backslashes in replacement text; if the replacement comes from someone else's input, return it from a function so none of its characters get a special meaning.
concepts.code:
import re

dates = "due 2026-10-17, paid 2026-09-30"
print(re.sub(r"(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})", r"\3/\2/\1", dates))
# due 17/10/2026, paid 30/09/2026

print(re.sub(r"(?P<key>\w+)=(?P<val>\w+)", r"\g<val>=\g<key>", "a=1 b=2"))  # 1=a 2=b

prices = "apple 1.50 USD, pear 0.75 USD"
to_eur = lambda m: f"{float(m[1]) * 0.86:.2f} EUR"
print(re.sub(r"(\d+\.\d+) USD", to_eur, prices))
# apple 1.29 EUR, pear 0.65 EUR

print(re.subn(r"\s+", " ", "too    many   spaces"))   # ('too many spaces', 2)

# JavaScript equivalent:
# "2026-10-17".replace(/(\d+)-(\d+)-(\d+)/, "$3/$2/$1")   // "17/10/2026"
takeaways: Python replacement text uses \1 or \g<name>; JavaScript uses $1 or $<name>
Pass a function when the replacement must be computed
JavaScript replace changes only the first match unless you use g or replaceAll
pitfalls: Writing \10 in Python meaning group 1 followed by 0; write \g<1>0.

quiz.explain: $1 and $2 insert the captured letters in swapped order.

concepts.name: Regex flavours: POSIX, PCRE, JS, Python, RE2
concepts.summary: Know the main regex dialects and how they differ in notation and features, so a pattern copied from one place works in another.
concepts.why: Patterns move between grep, editors, databases and languages, and small dialect differences cause silent mismatches.
concepts.body:
There is no single regex language; there are families with a shared core.

**POSIX** (basic and extended forms, BRE and ERE): grep, sed, awk and many databases' `~` matching. No `\d` or lazy quantifiers in the standard; bracket names like `[[:digit:]]` instead. Matching is leftmost-longest. In the basic form, `( ) { } + ? |` need backslashes.

**Perl and PCRE family**: PCRE2 (PHP, `grep -P`, nginx, R's `perl=TRUE`), Perl, Java, .NET, Ruby. The richest feature set, including every advanced construct in the later lessons.

**JavaScript (ECMAScript)**: Perl-like, with named groups and lookbehind (since ES2018) and the `u`/`v` Unicode modes, but missing a few advanced constructs and inline `(?x)`.

**Python `re`**: Perl-like; named groups written `(?P<name>...)` as well as `(?<name>...)` (3.12+), atomic groups and possessive quantifiers since 3.11, no `\p{...}` (the separate `regex` library adds it).

**RE2 family**: Go's `regexp`, Rust's `regex`, RE2 in C++ and in Google services. Matching time is guaranteed to grow only in step with the text, so there are **no backreferences and no lookarounds** (both covered later).

Practical rules: test the pattern in the engine that will run it (sites like regex101 let you pick the flavour), stick to the common core when a pattern must be portable, and check how your programming language treats backslashes in strings before the regex engine sees them.
concepts.code:
# the same idea, "one or more digits", in different tools
grep -E '[0-9]+' file.txt                 # POSIX ERE
grep '[0-9]\{1,\}' file.txt               # POSIX BRE
grep -P '\d+' file.txt                    # PCRE (GNU grep only)
sed -E 's/[0-9]+/N/g' file.txt            # ERE in sed
python3 -c 'import re; print(re.findall(r"\d+", "a1b22"))'   # ['1', '22']
node -e 'console.log("a1b22".match(/\d+/g))'                  # [ '1', '22' ]

# features that differ
#   lookbehind (?<=x)  : PCRE, Python, JS, Java   - not POSIX, Go or Rust
#   backreference \1   : POSIX BRE, PCRE, JS, Python - not Go or Rust
#   atomic (?>...)     : PCRE, Java, .NET, Python 3.11+ - not JS
takeaways: POSIX tools use [[:digit:]] and leftmost-longest matching
PCRE, Java, .NET, Python and JS share the Perl-style notation with differences at the edges
Go and Rust (RE2-style) trade backreferences and lookarounds for linear time
pitfalls: Copying a pattern with \d or lookarounds from a JavaScript answer into grep or Go and getting no matches or an error.

quiz.q: A pattern uses a backreference \1. Which engine will reject it?
quiz.explain: Go's regexp is RE2-style and omits backreferences to guarantee linear-time matching.

concepts.name: When not to use a regex
concepts.summary: Recognise jobs regexes do badly, such as nested structures, web pages, data files, full email checks and dates, and use proper tools instead.
concepts.why: Knowing a tool's limits is what keeps a clever one-liner from becoming a production bug.
concepts.body:
Classic regular expressions can only describe **regular languages**: kinds of text that can be recognised while remembering a fixed, limited amount of information. They can't keep count of nesting that may go arbitrarily deep, so they can't reliably match balanced parentheses, tags nested inside tags in a web page's HTML, or nested JSON data. (Some engines let a pattern refer to itself, but the result is unreadable and fragile.)

Use a real **parser**, code that reads a format by its full rules, instead:

- Web pages (HTML) and similar markup: an HTML parser such as BeautifulSoup or lxml.
- Data formats such as JSON, YAML or CSV: your language's ready-made reader for that format; CSV in particular has quoting rules a simple split gets wrong.
- Web addresses: `urllib.parse`, `new URL()`.
- Dates and numbers: `datetime.strptime` or a ready-made date tool will reject `2026-02-30`, which `\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}` happily accepts.

Some validations are better done loosely. A fully RFC-compliant email regex is enormous and still can't tell whether the address exists; check for something like `^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+$` and then send a confirmation email.

Regex shines for: searching code and logs, extracting pieces from loosely structured lines, quick validation of simple formats (IDs, postcodes, version numbers), and search-and-replace. If a pattern needs comments to explain, or grows beyond a line or two, consider a small hand-written parser or splitting the job into steps with ordinary text functions.
concepts.code:
import re, json
from datetime import datetime
from urllib.parse import urlparse

print(bool(re.fullmatch(r"\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}", "2026-02-30")))   # True (but not a date!)
try:
    datetime.strptime("2026-02-30", "%Y-%m-%d")
except ValueError as e:
    print("rejected:", e)            # rejected: day is out of range for month

doc = '{"a": {"b": [1, {"c": 2}]}}'
print(json.loads(doc)["a"]["b"][1]["c"])                         # 2

u = urlparse("https://ex.com:8080/p/a?q=1#top")
print(u.hostname, u.port, u.query)                               # ex.com 8080 q=1

print(bool(re.fullmatch(r"[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+", "ana@example.org")))  # True: loose check
takeaways: Regexes can't match arbitrarily nested structures
Use parsers for HTML, JSON, CSV, URLs and dates
Validate emails loosely and confirm them another way
pitfalls: Pulling data out of web pages with regexes that break as soon as the page's markup or spacing changes.

quiz.q: Why can't a classic regular expression check that parentheses are balanced to any depth?
options: It would need unbounded memory to count nesting depth
Regexes can't match the same character twice
quiz.explain: Regular languages are recognised with finite memory, and arbitrary nesting needs a counter or stack.

concepts.name: Lookahead and lookbehind
concepts.summary: Check what comes before or after a position with (?=...), (?!...), (?<=...) and (?<!...), without including it in the match.
concepts.why: Lookarounds express conditions like 'a number not followed by %' or 'must contain a digit' that plain patterns can't.
concepts.body:
**Lookarounds** are **zero-width assertions**, like `^` and `\b`: they check a condition at the current position and match no characters themselves. The difference is that you choose the condition, as a small pattern of its own.

- `X(?=Y)` positive lookahead: `X` only if followed by `Y`.
- `X(?!Y)` negative lookahead: `X` only if not followed by `Y`.
- `(?<=Y)X` positive lookbehind: `X` only if preceded by `Y`.
- `(?<!Y)X` negative lookbehind: `X` only if not preceded by `Y`.

Typical uses:

- Extract a value without its label: `(?<=price: )\d+`.
- Exclude a context: `\b\d+\b(?!%)` numbers that aren't percentages.
- Several independent conditions at one position: `^(?=.*\d)(?=.*[a-z]).{8,}$` requires a digit and a lowercase letter, in any order, in a string of at least 8 characters.
- Insert at a position: `re.sub(r"\B(?=(\d{3})+$)", ",", "1234567")` adds thousands separators.

Support differs. Python and PCRE require lookbehind to have a **fixed length** (PCRE2 allows alternatives of different fixed lengths, and from 10.43 also some length ranges); JavaScript and .NET allow any length. Go and Rust's standard engines have no lookarounds at all.
concepts.code:
import re

print(re.findall(r"(?<=price: )\d+", "price: 40, tax: 8"))       # ['40']
print(re.findall(r"\b\d+\b(?!%)", "5 apples, 20% off, 3 left"))  # ['5', '3']
print(re.findall(r"(?<!-)\b\d+", "a 5, b -3"))                   # ['5']

strong = re.compile(r"^(?=.*\d)(?=.*[a-z]).{8,}$")
print(bool(strong.match("password")))     # False: no digit
print(bool(strong.match("passw0rd")))     # True

print(re.sub(r"\B(?=(\d{3})+$)", ",", "1234567"))   # 1,234,567

try:
    re.compile(r"(?<=a+)b")
except re.error as e:
    print("error:", e)    # error: look-behind requires fixed-width pattern
takeaways: Lookarounds check a condition without consuming text
Chain lookaheads at ^ to require several things in any order
Lookbehind must be fixed-width in Python and most PCRE versions; Go and Rust have none
pitfalls: Expecting the lookahead's text to be part of the match or of a replaced span; it is only checked.

quiz.q: What does re.findall(r'\w+(?=:)', 'host: a, port: 80') return?
quiz.explain: The lookahead requires a colon after the word but doesn't include it in the match.

concepts.name: Backreferences inside the pattern
concepts.summary: Require the same text to appear twice with \1 or \k<name>, to find repeated words, matching quotes and paired tags.
concepts.why: Backreferences match 'the same thing again', which no character class or quantifier can express.
concepts.body:
A **backreference** in the pattern itself matches exactly the text a group captured earlier in the same match. `(\w+) \1` finds a doubled word like `the the`. Named versions are `(?P=name)` in Python and `\k<name>` in PCRE, JavaScript, Java and .NET.

Common uses:

- Repeated words in prose: `\b(\w+)\s+\1\b` with the ignore-case flag.
- Matching quotes: `(["'])(.*?)\1` accepts `"x"` and `'x'` but not `"x'`.
- Paired simple tags: `<(\w+)>.*?</\1>` for non-nested tags.
- Repeated characters: `(.)\1{2,}` finds any character repeated three or more times.

Things to know:

- A backreference matches the **text**, not the pattern: `(\d)\1` matches `55`, not `56`.
- If the group didn't participate, Python fails the backreference, while JavaScript lets it match the empty string.
- Backreferences take regexes beyond what classic regular expressions can describe: in the worst case no known method matches them quickly (the problem is NP-hard), which is why RE2, Go and Rust leave them out and why they can be slow in grep.
- Don't confuse them with `\1` in the replacement text of `re.sub`, which is a different (simpler) mechanism.
concepts.code: import re text = "This is the the test, and and it works" print(re.findall(r"\b(\w+)\s+\1\b", text)) # ['the', 'and'] print(re.findall(r'(["\'])(.*?)\1', ' "a" \'b\' "c\' ')) # [('"', 'a'), ("'", 'b')] print(bool(re.fullmatch(r"<(\w+)>.*?", "bold"))) # True print(bool(re.fullmatch(r"<(\w+)>.*?", "bold"))) # False print(re.findall(r"((.)\2{2,})", "aaxyyyyz111")) # [('yyyy', 'y'), ('111', '1')] print(bool(re.fullmatch(r"(?P\d)(?P=d)", "55"))) # True
takeaways: \1 inside the pattern matches the same text group 1 captured
Named form: (?P=name) in Python, \k<name> elsewhere
Backreferences are unsupported in RE2, Go and Rust and can be slow
pitfalls: Expecting (\d)\1 to match any two digits; it matches only a repeated digit.

quiz.explain: The backreference repeats the exact text the group matched, so the two halves must be identical.

concepts.name: Unicode in regular expressions
concepts.summary: Match international text correctly: Unicode-aware \w and \d, \p{L} Unicode properties, the JavaScript u and v flags, and graphemes versus code points.
concepts.why: User names, addresses and emoji break ASCII-only patterns in ways that are easy to miss in testing.
concepts.body:
Modern engines operate on **code points**, but what they treat as a letter or digit depends on flags and flavour:

- Python 3 `str` patterns are Unicode-aware by default: `\w` matches `é` and `ж`, `\d` matches all decimal digits. `re.ASCII` restricts them.
- JavaScript `\w` and `\d` are ASCII-only even with the `u` flag.
- `\p{...}` **property classes** select by Unicode category or writing system: `\p{L}` any letter, `\p{Lu}` uppercase, `\p{N}` numbers, `\p{Script=Greek}`. They work in PCRE, Java, .NET, Rust, and JavaScript with `u` or `v`. Python's `re` lacks them; the separate `regex` library adds them.
- JavaScript's `u` flag makes `.` match a whole astral code point such as an emoji instead of half of one (JavaScript stores such characters as two halves, a surrogate pair). The `v` flag (ES2024) adds class set operations like `[\p{L}--[a-z]]` and string properties like `\p{RGI_Emoji}`.

A user-perceived character (a **grapheme**) can be several code points: `é` may be `e` plus a combining accent, and a family emoji is several code points joined by zero-width joiners. `.` matches one code point, so it can split them. PCRE and Python's `regex` library support `\X` for a grapheme cluster.

Normalise text first (`unicodedata.normalize("NFC", s)`) so that visually identical strings compare and match the same way.
concepts.code:
import re, unicodedata

print(re.findall(r"\w+", "café naïve Жук"))           # ['café', 'naïve', 'Жук']
print(re.findall(r"\w+", "café", re.ASCII))           # ['caf']

decomposed = "café"                              # e + combining acute
print(len(decomposed), re.fullmatch(r"\w{4}", decomposed))   # 5 None
nfc = unicodedata.normalize("NFC", decomposed)
print(len(nfc), bool(re.fullmatch(r"\w{4}", nfc)))   # 4 True

# JavaScript (node):
#   "Ünïcödé 42".match(/\p{L}+/gu)      -> [ 'Ünïcödé' ]
#   "Ünïcödé".match(/\w+/g)             -> [ 'n', 'c', 'd' ]   ASCII-only \w
#   "😀".match(/./g).length              -> 2   (surrogate halves)
#   "😀".match(/./gu).length             -> 1
takeaways: Python's \w and \d are Unicode-aware; JavaScript's are ASCII-only
\p{L} and friends match by Unicode property (JS needs u or v)
Normalise to NFC before matching; graphemes can span several code points
pitfalls: Validating names with [A-Za-z]+, which rejects José, Zoë and most of the world.

quiz.q: In JavaScript, which pattern matches a word in any alphabet?
quiz.explain: \p{L} is the Unicode letter property, available with the u or v flag; \w is ASCII-only in JavaScript.

concepts.name: Atomic groups and possessive quantifiers
concepts.summary: Stop the engine from backtracking into a group with (?>...) or possessive quantifiers *+ ++ ?+, for speed and to rule out unwanted matches.
concepts.why: They are the precise tool for making some patterns fail fast instead of exploring thousands of useless paths.
concepts.body:
When a backtracking engine fails later in the pattern, it returns to earlier quantifiers and tries giving back characters. Usually that is what makes greedy matching work. Sometimes you know giving back can never help, and you want to forbid it.

- An **atomic group** `(?>...)` matches like a normal group, but once it has matched, the engine throws away its backtracking positions. If the rest of the pattern fails, the group won't try a shorter alternative.
- A **possessive quantifier** `*+`, `++`, `?+`, `{m,n}+` is shorthand for an atomic group around a greedy quantifier: `\d++` equals `(?>\d+)`.

Example: `\d+0` matches `1230` because `\d+` gives back the final `0`. `\d++0` never matches, since `\d++` keeps all digits. That shows the semantic difference: these constructs can change **whether** a pattern matches, not just how fast.

They shine at preventing catastrophic backtracking: in `"(?:[^"\\]++|\\.)*+"` no input can make the engine try the same characters again in different ways.

Support: PCRE, Perl, Java, .NET, Ruby, and Python 3.11+. JavaScript has neither; a lookahead with a backreference `(?=(\d+))\1` imitates an atomic group there.
concepts.code:
import re   # Python 3.11+

print(re.fullmatch(r"\d+0", "1230"))          # <re.Match ...match='1230'>
print(re.fullmatch(r"\d++0", "1230"))         # None: \d++ won't give back the 0
print(re.fullmatch(r"(?>\d+)0", "1230"))      # None: same thing as an atomic group

# a quoted string with escapes, no possible double-matching of characters
qstr = re.compile(r'"(?:[^"\\]++|\\.)*+"')
print(qstr.findall(r'say "hi \"there\"" and "bye"'))
# ['"hi \\"there\\""', '"bye"']

# emulating an atomic group in JavaScript-compatible syntax
print(re.fullmatch(r"(?=(\d+))\1[0]", "1230"))  # None, like (?>\d+)0
takeaways: (?>...) and possessive quantifiers never give back what they matched
They can change whether a pattern matches, not only its speed
Available in PCRE, Java, .NET and Python 3.11+, not JavaScript
pitfalls: Making a quantifier possessive when the rest of the pattern needs some of those characters, so it can never match.

quiz.q: Does a++b match the string aaab?
options: No, possessive quantifiers can't match a
quiz.explain: a++ takes all the a's and keeps them, but b still follows, so no backtracking is needed and it matches.

concepts.name: How a backtracking engine matches
concepts.summary: Follow how PCRE-style engines try each start position, branch on quantifiers and alternatives, and backtrack on failure.
concepts.why: Reading a pattern the way the engine executes it explains surprising matches and is the basis of performance work.
concepts.body:
Most engines in languages (PCRE, Perl, Java, .NET, Python, JavaScript) are **backtracking** matchers. Conceptually:

- They try the pattern at position 0 of the subject, then 1, then 2, and report the first position where it matches. That is why the result is the **leftmost** match.
- At each choice point (a quantifier deciding how many to take, an alternation choosing a branch, an optional item) they pick the preferred option, greedy means "more first", and push the alternatives onto a stack.
- When a later part fails, they pop the most recent choice and try its next option. Only when every choice at this start position is exhausted do they move the start forward.

Consequences:

- Alternation is ordered: the first alternative that leads to an overall match wins, not the longest.
- The cost of a failed match can be the product of the choices of every quantifier involved.
- Engines optimise heavily: a pattern starting with fixed text jumps straight to occurrences of it, anchored patterns try only one start position, and "first character" sets skip impossible positions. That's why anchoring and leading literals speed things up.

Step-by-step views such as regex101's, or PCRE2's callouts, show every step and are the best way to build intuition.
concepts.code:
import re, time

# matching a.*b against "aXXbYYb" (greedy):
#   a    -> matches at 0
#   .*   -> takes "XXbYYb" (to the end)
#   b    -> fails at end; backtrack: .* gives back 'b' -> b matches -> "aXXbYYb"
print(re.search(r"a.*b", "aXXbYYb").group())     # aXXbYYb
print(re.search(r"a.*?b", "aXXbYYb").group())    # aXXb (lazy: fewest first)

# leftmost wins over longest
print(re.search(r"b|abc", "abc").group())        # abc  (position 0 tried first)

# anchoring lets a failing search stop early
s = "x" * 200_000
t = time.perf_counter(); re.search(r"y\d", s); a = time.perf_counter() - t
t = time.perf_counter(); re.match(r"y\d", s); b = time.perf_counter() - t
print(a > b)                                     # True: match() tries only position 0
takeaways: The engine tries each start position in turn: the first that succeeds wins
Every quantifier and alternation is a choice point that may be revisited
Fixed leading text and anchors let the engine skip impossible positions
pitfalls: Assuming the engine finds the longest match, as POSIX tools do; backtracking engines find the first that works.

quiz.q: A backtracking engine applies (a|ab)(c|bcd) to 'abcd'. What does it match?
quiz.explain: First it tries a then c (fails at b), then a then bcd, which succeeds, giving abcd.

concepts.name: Catastrophic backtracking and ReDoS
concepts.summary: Spot nested or overlapping quantifiers that take exponential time on failing input, and fix them with stricter patterns, atomic groups or a linear engine.
concepts.why: One bad pattern on a server can be frozen by a 30-character string; this has taken down major sites.
concepts.body:
**Catastrophic backtracking** happens when a pattern can match the same text in exponentially many ways, and the overall match then **fails**. The engine dutifully tries every split before giving up. The classic shape is a nested quantifier like `(a+)+$` or overlapping alternatives like `(a|a)*` or `(\w|\d)+`. On `"aaaa...a!"` each extra `a` roughly doubles the work.

Real-world variants hide in checks of typed-in text: `^(\w+\s?)*$`, email patterns with nested groups, or `(.*,)*` for comma-separated lines. When an attacker controls the input, this is a **ReDoS** (regular expression denial of service).

How to fix or prevent it:

- Make alternatives **mutually exclusive** and each character matchable in only one way: `^\w+(?:\s\w+)*$` instead of `^(\w+\s?)*$`.
- Use **possessive quantifiers** or **atomic groups** so the engine can't re-split: `(?:\w++\s?)*+`.
- Limit the length of the text before matching, and set a time limit where the platform allows (.NET `MatchTimeout`, Java via interruptible input).
- For untrusted patterns or inputs, use a linear-time engine (RE2, Go, Rust, or `google-re2` for Python).
- Check automatically: tools like `safe-regex`, CodeQL and `recheck` find vulnerable patterns.
concepts.code:
import re, time

evil = re.compile(r"^(\w+\s?)*$")
safe = re.compile(r"^\w+(?:\s\w+)*$")

for n in (18, 20, 22):
    s = "a" * n + "!"                   # fails at the very end
    t = time.perf_counter(); evil.match(s); e = time.perf_counter() - t
    t = time.perf_counter(); safe.match(s); f = time.perf_counter() - t
    print(n, f"evil {e:.3f}s", f"safe {f:.6f}s")
# 18 evil 0.08s  safe 0.000008s
# 20 evil 0.25s  ...  each extra character roughly doubles the time
# 22 evil 1.0s

print(bool(safe.match("hello big world")))    # True, same language as intended
takeaways: Nested or overlapping quantifiers plus a failing match = exponential time
Make each character matchable in only one way, or use atomic/possessive constructs
For text from strangers, cap lengths or use a linear-time engine
pitfalls: Testing a pattern only on inputs that match; catastrophic cases appear on near-misses that fail at the end.

quiz.q: Which pattern is vulnerable to catastrophic backtracking?
quiz.explain: The nested + lets a run of a's be split between the inner and outer quantifier in exponentially many ways.

concepts.name: Automata engines: NFA, DFA and linear time
concepts.summary: How Thompson NFA simulation and DFAs match in time linear in the input, why they drop backreferences, and how RE2, Go and Rust use them.
concepts.why: Choosing an engine with guarantees is the robust fix for untrusted patterns and huge inputs.
concepts.body:
A regular expression without backreferences can be turned into a **finite automaton**: states connected by character transitions.

- A **Thompson NFA** has a small number of states, one per pattern element. Instead of trying one path and backtracking, the matcher tracks the **set** of all states the automaton could be in, advancing them together for each input character. The cost is at most O(pattern size x input size), with no exponential blow-up.
- A **DFA** precomputes, for each set of NFA states, where every input character leads. Matching is then one table lookup per character, the fastest possible, but the number of DFA states can grow exponentially, so engines build them only as needed and limit how many they keep (grep and RE2 do this).

What you lose: backreferences (they need to remember captured text) and, in RE2, Go and Rust, lookarounds. Capturing groups are possible with extra machinery (tagged NFAs, a one-pass or bounded-backtracking engine for small inputs), which is why sub-match extraction is slower than a yes/no test in those libraries.

Leftmost-first semantics like Perl's can be imitated by giving the NFA's parallel paths priorities, which RE2 and Rust do, so most patterns behave identically apart from the missing features.

Use these engines when patterns or inputs are untrusted, or inputs are very large; use a backtracking engine when you genuinely need its extra features.
takeaways: NFA simulation tracks all possible states at once: linear time, no backtracking
DFAs are faster but built only as needed, because they can grow huge
RE2, Go and Rust trade backreferences and lookarounds for guaranteed speed
pitfalls: Porting a pattern with backreferences to Go and having MustCompile stop the program with an error when it runs.

quiz.q: Why can't a DFA-based engine support backreferences?
options: A backreference needs to remember arbitrary captured text, which a finite set of states can't
Backreferences are only valid in POSIX
quiz.explain: The language matched by (\w+)\1 is not regular; recognising it requires unbounded memory.
